name: nihilism
quote: Life sucks and then you die.
description: A pattern of belief that there's no meaning to life, so our actions don't matter.
perceptions: Human social systems are constructed in an arbitrary way.

guidance.description: People stressed by the search for meaning can find comfort in 'sunny' nihilism.
If you find nihilism more depressing than relieving, here are some references to consider:

variations.name: moral nihilism
variations.description: A pattern of belief that human morals are arbitrary and there are no objective moral truths.
perceptions: Human moral systems are constructed in an arbitrary way.
Living in accordance with one of them is for sheeple.

variations.name: knowledge nihilism
variations.description: A pattern of belief that there are no objective truths.
perceptions: Human knowledge systems are constructed in an arbitrary way.
We can't be absolutely certain about anything.

variations.name: cosmic nihilism
variations.description: A pattern of belief that the universe is meaningless and indifferent to the existence or non-existence of humans.
perceptions: Human beings are not the pinnacle product of the universe.
We are a by-product that cannot expect special treatment.

comparisons.description: The most common usage of 'nihilism' refers to a human life having no inherent meaning. The other forms deny other certainties: 'moral nihilism' denies absolute moral truths, 'knowledge nihilism' denies absolute truths of any kind, and 'cosmic nihilism' denies that the universe has inherent meaning, nor does it particularly care about humanity.

commentaries.quote: If we believe in nothing, if nothing has any meaning and if we can affirm no values whatsoever, then everything is possible and nothing has any importance.
Nihilism might be more intellectually consistent, but perhaps the intellect should not be the only source of truth.

For the past few years, I’ve been consumed by nihilism. But my descent into the controversial philosophy hasn’t been a grim road of despair and hopelessness. Quite the opposite. It’s become one of the most illuminating and fortifying parts of my life.

Though nihilism has been relentlessly criticized for overemphasizing the dark side of human experience, it might be equally true that this overemphasis represents a needed counterbalance to shallow optimism and arrogant confidence in human power.
Everything in the world displeases me: but, above all, my displeasure in everything displeases me.

Strict reliance on the intellect to make sense of the world leads ineluctably to despair, rubbing our noses in the inescapability of pain and death. As a rule, people need a sense of order, meaning, and certainty to feel hopeful and engaged in the world.
commentaries.attribution: Charles Harper Webb Ph.D. in psychologytoday.com
